title: End Of The World

jokes.text: Andy bowing to Leslie when presenting Herb
jokes.setup: Andy is introducing a citizen to Leslie in a professional government setting
jokes.punchline: Andy bows like a medieval servant, totally incongruous with his role as a city employee
jokes.explanation: Perfect Andy character beat — his childlike deference and inability to read professional norms is his defining trait. 'As you wish, ma'am' seals it with a fairy-tale register. The Leslie correction 'you don't need to bow' grounds it. Works beautifully in one exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Leslie Knope, I'd like to present to you... *bows*

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, you don't have to bow.

jokes.text: Leslie's response to being told the world is ending: 'Oh, nuts. You're sure it's tomorrow?'
jokes.setup: A citizen solemnly warns Leslie the world will end at dawn
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response is cartoonishly mild — 'Oh, nuts' — and her follow-up is purely logistical, as if she's double-checking a meeting time
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Leslie Knope characterization compressed into four words. 'Oh, nuts' is the perfect Leslie expletive — wholesome, mild, and bureaucratically unflappable. The follow-up question treats apocalyptic prophecy as a scheduling conflict. High character integration: only Leslie would respond this way. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The all-night vigils are annoying, but you know what's really gross? They don't have a sewage system. So during the apocalypse, they're just going to the bathroom in holes in the ground. Holes! In the ground!

jokes.text: Talking-head confessional: 'Turns out, when you think the world is ending, you don't aim so carefully in the Porta-Potties.'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains the cult has a history of all-night vigils in the park
jokes.punchline: The practical civic nightmare this creates — bad Porta-Potty aim — is delivered with total bureaucratic seriousness
jokes.explanation: A brilliant left turn from the existential to the sanitation. The specificity of 'Porta-Potties' and the cause-effect logic ('when you think the world is ending') is genuinely clever writing. Leslie's deadpan civic concern makes it funnier — this is her real worry about the cult.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why do they call themselves 'The Reasonableists'?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The twisted logic is so backwards it's actually clever.

jokes.text: The cult calls itself 'The Reasonableists' so critics will seem like they're attacking something reasonable
jokes.setup: Ben asks why the doomsday cult would call themselves 'The Reasonableists'
jokes.punchline: Leslie explains it's a rhetorical shield: critics end up sounding like they're against reason itself
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical writing about cult branding and rhetorical manipulation. Ben's genuine reaction 'That's weirdly brilliant' is the right straight-man beat. The concept is original and has real intellectual teeth. Not as character-specific as some jokes but the writing is crisp.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: There's nothing to worry about. The cult's predictions are never accurate.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Although, they did correctly predict that Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie would break up.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So maybe we should be concerned.

jokes.text: Ben's response 'That's weirdly brilliant' to the Reasonableists cult naming strategy
jokes.setup: Leslie explains the cult's manipulative naming strategy
jokes.punchline: Ben, the rational bureaucrat, can't help but genuinely admire the rhetorical cleverness of a doomsday cult
jokes.explanation: A well-placed reaction that subverts the expected straight-man dismissal. Ben admiring cult strategy is a small but effective character beat. Economy is excellent — three words carry the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Lance Armstrong dumped Sheryl Crow. Can you believe that? I mean, she's amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's crazy. He's an idiot.

jokes.text: The only bad thing that ever happened on past doomsday dates was Lance Armstrong dumping Sheryl Crow — 'That was a tragic day. LIVESTRONG.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reassures everyone that past doomsday predictions resulted in nothing bad happening
jokes.punchline: She names the one 'tragedy' — a celebrity breakup — then solemnly invokes Lance Armstrong's cancer charity slogan
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'nothing bad happened' to celebrity gossip to 'LIVESTRONG' is a perfect three-beat joke. The solemnity of 'LIVESTRONG' as a response to the Armstrong-Crow breakup is absurdist Leslie logic at its best. High quotability, strong character integration — this is exactly the kind of non sequitur Leslie would treat with complete sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going with you. I need to see this made-up planet name 'Nutbrain' for myself.

jokes.text: 'I live on planet Nut Bran. Bran and nuts are very helpful for your colon.'
jokes.setup: Leslie dismisses the cult by saying they 'live on planet Nutbrain'
jokes.punchline: Herb mishears it as 'Nut Bran,' pivots to a dietary endorsement of fiber for colon health
jokes.explanation: The misunderstanding creates a nice malapropism beat. The colon follow-up is the escalation that makes it work — he's not just mishearing, he's enthusiastically advocating for fiber. The non sequitur from apocalypse to digestive health is absurdly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The cult lives on planet Nutbrain.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Nutbrain? That's actually really good advice. I've been eating too much dairy.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head about not hanging out with Ben: 'Big deal. Lots of people don't hang out. Jerry and April. Obama and Madonna, probably.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to downplay the awkwardness of not hanging out with Ben post-breakup
jokes.punchline: She lists examples of people who don't hang out — coworkers who barely interact, then wildly escalates to 'Obama and Madonna, probably'
jokes.explanation: The list joke escalates perfectly: Jerry/April (believable coworker distance) → Obama/Madonna (completely absurd celebrity non-pairing). The 'probably' is the key word — Leslie's breezy confidence in a speculation she has no basis for. Strong Leslie voice, good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben and I hang out all the time. We're very close.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You guys haven't hung out in like three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not true. We grabbed coffee last week.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That was two months ago.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, we text constantly.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You don't text him.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fine. But if Ben and I were a celebrity couple, we'd be called Lesben, and we'd be huge.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You'd also need Ben to actually know you were in a relationship with him.

jokes.text: 'We're in good company.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just claimed Obama and Madonna probably don't hang out either
jokes.punchline: She sincerely concludes this puts her and Ben in the same category as the President and a pop icon
jokes.explanation: A functional button to joke #8. Works as a tag but doesn't stand alone — it's the capper that makes the prior absurdist list land harder. Modest but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Dude, we're gonna be rich! Five grand each!

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yeah! We're gonna start our own company!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We'll be right up there with the greats.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yeah! Like Enron!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Lehman Brothers!

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Blockbuster!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jamba Juice.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: What? Jamba Juice is still around.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Not the way I manage money.

jokes.text: Entertainment 720 is eulogized alongside Pets.com, Blockbuster, and Ask Jeeves
jokes.setup: Tom and Jean-Ralphio discover Entertainment 720 is bankrupt with only $5,000 left each
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio places their failed company in the pantheon of legendary corporate failures — Pets.com, Blockbuster, Ask Jeeves
jokes.explanation: Comparing Entertainment 720 to dot-com bubble casualties is a sharp satirical choice. The list is well-curated — all three examples are culturally legible failures. Tom and Jean-Ralphio treating this as a badge of honor rather than shame is perfect character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My company is just like Ask Jeeves. We had a great idea, we were ahead of our time, and now we're completely obsolete and nobody remembers us.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ask Jeeves was a search engine where you asked a butler questions. A butler! For the internet! How did anyone think that was a good idea?

jokes.text: 'My company is no better than a company where you ask a fake butler to Google things for you.'
jokes.setup: Tom is reeling from Entertainment 720's collapse and its comparison to Ask Jeeves
jokes.punchline: Tom's self-aware summary of Ask Jeeves — 'a company where you ask a fake butler to Google things for you' — is both accurate and devastatingly funny as self-indictment
jokes.explanation: Tom briefly achieves genuine self-awareness, which is funnier than his usual delusion. The Ask Jeeves description is sharp and accurate — it IS a company where you ask a fake butler to Google things for you. The joke works on two levels: mocking Ask Jeeves AND Tom's equivalence with them.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: What should we do next?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I'm thinking we get hit by a bus, collect the insurance money, and use that to start our business.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not a business plan.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: What? It's foolproof!

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's plan: invest the money, accidentally get run over by a city bus, and start a hip hop label
jokes.setup: Tom and Jean-Ralphio are discussing what to do with their remaining $10,000
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio casually includes 'accidentally get run over by a city bus' as a middle step in his business plan, suggesting insurance fraud as an obvious pivot strategy
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio at his peak — the casual insertion of 'accidentally get run over by a city bus' as a business step, with no elaboration, is perfectly absurdist. It's both a character reveal (he's done this before or seriously considered it) and a dark comedy beat. The word 'accidentally' doing enormous heavy lifting. High originality, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yo, this party's gonna be straight up Fire Marshal Bill!

jokes.text: 'A party for the end of the world.' / 'You had me at every dime we have left.'
jokes.setup: Tom pitches throwing one last party with everything they have left
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's 'you had me at...' subverts the Jerry Maguire cliché — instead of being moved by a romantic declaration, he's moved by the promise of spending all remaining money
jokes.explanation: The subversion of 'you had me at hello' with the punchline being financial recklessness is a good character beat for Jean-Ralphio. His values are exactly backwards from the romantic ideal the phrase invokes. Functional misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo, yo, yo! Swag!

jokes.text: 'Because I'm in like Lara Flynn Boyle from The Practice.'
jokes.setup: Tom pitches throwing a last party with all their remaining money — 'you had me at every dime we have left'
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio adds an obscure, non-sequitur celebrity comparison to express enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Jean-Ralphio non sequitur — the random 90s TV reference is his voice exactly. But the joke is more weird than funny; the Lara Flynn Boyle reference is obscure enough that many viewers won't get it, reducing impact. Works as character texture more than an actual joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What should we do tonight?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We could go to Sweetums and get a pretzel. Then we could go home and watch TV until we fall asleep. Then tomorrow we wake up and do it all over again until we die.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's celebration: 'Diddly, diddly, diddly, diddly, diddly, diddly, swag.'
jokes.setup: They've just decided to throw a party with all their money
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's expression of excitement is six 'diddlys' followed by 'swag' — a completely meaningless yet somehow triumphant verbal celebration
jokes.explanation: Pure Jean-Ralphio id — the repetition of 'diddly' followed by 'swag' is nonsense that somehow perfectly captures his character. It's a character laugh, not a constructed joke. Fun but not crafted.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We do the same thing every night.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's what relationships are, April. It's about finding someone you love and doing the same thing over and over until one of you dies.

jokes.text: April and Andy's nightly routine: pizza, Xbox, prank calls, getting hammered, making out — 'We do that every night.' / 'That's because repetition is the key to a good marriage.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks what they should do for the night as if it's an open question
jokes.punchline: April reveals this is literally every night of their marriage, and Andy responds with a marriage tip that sounds like profound wisdom but is just lazy logic
jokes.explanation: The joke builds from a revealed routine to Andy's pseudo-profound 'repetition is the key to a good marriage' — which sounds like a platitude but is just him defending laziness. The list of activities is funny on its own (escalating from pizza to making out), and April's flat delivery of 'We do that every night' is a perfect deadpan. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I want to remake 'Son of the Mask' and get it right this time.

jokes.text: Andy's bucket list includes remaking Kazaam with Shaquille O'Neal 'where he plays a genie, and I'd like to get it right'
jokes.setup: Andy reveals his bucket list for what might be their last night on Earth
jokes.punchline: Among legitimate-ish items (skydiving, lottery, unicycle) is the goal to remake Kazaam and 'get it right' — implying Andy has strong artistic opinions about the 1996 Shaq film
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. 'I'd like to get it right' implies Andy has genuine artistic dissatisfaction with the original Kazaam, treating a notoriously bad children's movie as a noble creative project awaiting its definitive version. The specificity (Shaquille O'Neal, playing a genie) is perfect — it's not just 'remake a bad movie' but this exact film, with this exact actor, in this exact role. Absurdist logic delivered with complete sincerity, and wholly unique to Andy Dwyer. Among the funniest character jokes in the series.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm gonna show you how to act classy on a plane. First, you gotta lean back like this and say 'These pretzels are making me thirsty,' but like, super annoyed about it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Then when the flight attendant comes by, you go 'Excuse me, do you have any other nuts? These are so pedestrian.' Even though you love pretzels and you're gonna eat all of them.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And when you land, you take off your sunglasses real slow and say 'That was a bumpy flight. I'm used to private jets.' You're not used to private jets.

jokes.text: Andy mimes looking out a first-class airplane window at passersby on the ground — 'When people are walking by, be like this'
jokes.setup: Andy is rattling off bucket list items including 'fly first class on a plane'
jokes.punchline: He physically acts out the specific thing he wants to do in first class — look down condescendingly at pedestrians — revealing that flying first class is purely about the social status signal
jokes.explanation: A visual gag that requires the physical performance — Andy's mime of looking down his nose at ground-level people is funnier than the words alone. The joke reveals Andy's conception of first-class travel is entirely about the power dynamic, not comfort. Strong visual beat with good character insight.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Eighteen dollars and four cents. That's... that's basically a million dollars.

jokes.text: April chooses one bucket list item: holding $1,000 in cash. They withdraw exactly $1,000, and it takes two counting attempts to get to the anticlimactic total
jokes.setup: April picks the bucket list goal of holding $1,000 cash in your hands, which Andy counts out with great ceremony
jokes.punchline: The bank account has $18.04 remaining — they spent nearly everything — and the first count of $998 is fumbled, requiring a redo, all for the modest thrill of holding four figures in cash
jokes.explanation: The joke is the gap between the grandeur implied (an item on your last-night bucket list) and the modesty of the payoff (touching a thousand dollars). The '$18.04 left in the bank account' detail is a nice kicker. The fumbled first count adds a layer of low-stakes incompetence that fits Andy perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, you broke it into smaller bills?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's the same thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No it's not! Look at all this money!

jokes.text: Andy's reaction to holding the $1,000: extreme disappointment, then euphoria after a recount — 'That's super disappointing... Yes! Now this is what I imagined.'
jokes.setup: Andy counts out $1,000 in cash, arriving at $998 the first time
jokes.punchline: His devastation at $998 is total, and his complete turnaround joy at $1,000 (a $2 difference) is equally total — revealing he has no sense of proportion
jokes.explanation: Andy's emotional binary (complete devastation / complete euphoria) over a $2 difference is funny because it's so true to his character. The visual of his face falling and then erupting must be remarkable. Good use of escalation via emotional over-reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Have you ever seen this much cash?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I literally just gave it to you.

jokes.text: After the recount, Andy erupts with 'Yes! Now, this is what I imagined!' — the second count of identical bills somehow satisfies him
jokes.setup: Andy was disappointed by the first $1,000 count; April recounts the exact same money
jokes.punchline: Andy is now fully satisfied — the second count of the same bills triggers the response the first didn't, for no rational reason
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the disappointment beat — Andy's satisfaction has no rational basis, which is perfect. The joke is that literally nothing changed except Andy's perception. Character-specific and well-earned from the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have cash! Real money in my pocket!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what I could do with this? I could buy a soda. Or two sodas!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, forget sodas. I'm gonna use this to get pennies. Thousands of pennies.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna fill a bathtub with pennies and just roll around in them like I'm some kind of copper-based Scrooge McDuck.

jokes.text: 'Have you ever seen this much cash in your entire life?' / 'I just handed it to you.'
jokes.setup: Andy holds the $1,000 and asks April with awe if she's ever seen this much cash
jokes.punchline: April's flat reminder that she literally just handed it to him punctures his wonder completely
jokes.explanation: Six words from April destroy Andy's sense of wonder. The economy is excellent — April's comeback is as short as possible while being maximally deflating. This is a perfect straight-man/fool exchange, and the fact that she DID just hand it to him makes the burn undeniable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Look, I don't care what people believe in. If they want to worship a golden calf or think the government is run by lizard people, that's their business.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm a live-and-let-live kind of man.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's very progressive of you, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, they also gave me a significant tax write-off.

jokes.text: 'Nickels. I want nickels. A billion nickels!'
jokes.setup: April has just deflated Andy's wonder at holding cash
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately pivots to wanting a billion nickels — not more dollars, specifically nickels, and specifically a billion of them — which is both impractical and slightly menacing in volume
jokes.explanation: The specific denomination (nickels) and the specific quantity (a billion) is great absurdist specificity. Andy's brain works in strange loops — cash disappointment → want more → but specifically nickels → a billion of them. Classic Andy escalation logic.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm making flutes for the ceremony. I have three sizes: small, medium, and large. Small flute costs $50, medium flute costs $100, and large flute costs $150.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: he finds the cult ridiculous BUT respects religious freedom AND they use flutes — 'Flutes are $80 apiece, and recorders are $150.'
jokes.setup: Ron dismisses the Reasonableists as ridiculous, invokes the Founding Fathers to defend their right to practice, then reveals his actual interest: he sells the flutes they use in ceremonies
jokes.punchline: The principle of religious freedom is immediately monetized — Ron's libertarianism is entirely self-serving commerce disguised as high-minded philosophy
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes because it does so much work so efficiently. Ron's three-step logic — (1) they're ridiculous, (2) I defend their freedom, (3) they require flutes and I sell flutes — is a perfect structural reveal. It skewers libertarian principle as enlightened self-interest. The price list delivered with total deadpan ('$80 apiece, recorders are $150') is quintessential Ron. Exceptional character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: Ron, I'd like to buy those flutes from you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: They're not for sale.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: I'll write you a check.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A check?

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: Yes, post-dated for after the world ends.

jokes.text: Ron sells a flute to a Zorpie who asks 'Would you take a check? You can cash it tomorrow.' Ron: 'Sure.'
jokes.setup: A Zorpie buys a flute from Ron, notes the world ends tomorrow so the check will be cashable then
jokes.punchline: Ron accepts without hesitation — because if the world ends, the check doesn't matter, and if it doesn't, he gets paid. Either way Ron wins, and he knows it.
jokes.explanation: A perfect two-word punchline. The Zorpie's logic is the setup up (the check is good because tomorrow the world ends, so he'll definitely be around to cash it), but Ron's 'Sure' acknowledges none of the theological stakes — he's just a merchant. The joke rewards anyone paying attention to the irony. Economy score of 9: one word does maximum comedy work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We have a VIP section, obviously. But then we have a Super VIP section. And then we have an Ultra VIP section. And then we have a section that's so VIP, that even I can't go in there.

jokes.text: Entertainment 720's party has a VIP area, double VIP, triple VIP, Centurion Club Elite VIP — 'No one is allowed in there. Not even us.'
jokes.setup: Tom describes the party's layout as an escalating series of VIP sections
jokes.punchline: The highest tier — Centurion Club Elite VIP, sponsored by SoBe Lifewater — is so exclusive that even the founders can't enter it
jokes.explanation: The escalation from VIP to Centurion Club Elite is perfectly satirical of club culture's hierarchy absurdism. The kicker 'Not even us. Mmm-mmm.' is great — Tom and Jean-Ralphio are proud of having created a space they cannot access. The SoBe Lifewater sponsorship adds a layer of bathetically unhip corporate partnership. Strong construction.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey, how's it going?

dialogue.speaker: Bouncer
dialogue.line: You're banned.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Right, right. Well, I'm actually the owner now, so...

jokes.text: The bouncer Keith — 'He actually once tossed me out of a club three years ago. Water under the bridge.'
jokes.setup: Tom introduces the huge scary bouncers he hired for the party, cheerfully greeting one by name
jokes.punchline: Keith personally ejected Tom from a club three years ago, and Tom has now hired him — treating the humiliation as no big deal
jokes.explanation: Small but effective Tom character beat — his social aspirations and selective memory work together. The 'Water under the bridge' is perfect Tom bravado hiding past social failure. The joke reveals that Tom has been thrown out of clubs, which tells us a lot about his history.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is actually perfect. Now I can set up all the surprises before everyone gets here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Plus, I get some alone time to mentally prepare myself for all the socializing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? This is the best party I've ever thrown.

jokes.text: 'No one shows up to a good party on time. If anyone had actually shown up right now, the whole party would have been ruined.'
jokes.setup: The party begins and absolutely no one is there
jokes.punchline: Tom and Jean-Ralphio reassure each other (and themselves) that empty parties at start time are actually signs of quality
jokes.explanation: A nice cringe-adjacent beat — they're clearly panicking but inverting the logic to reassure themselves. The second sentence ('Would have been a disaster') overcommits so hilariously that it becomes self-parody. Classic Tom cope.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: No, no, no. That's too long. How about: 'Local Woman Initiates Positive Community Change Through Dedicated Civic Engagement and Strategic Partnership Development'?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's longer.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: Well, it's more accurate.

jokes.text: Leslie tells reporter Shauna that Chris and Ben are at the vigil because she 'had nothing better to do, which probably says more about me than them'
jokes.setup: Shauna asks Leslie whether the presence of City Manager's office staff signals concern about the cult
jokes.punchline: Leslie accidentally includes herself in the admission, revealing she also has nothing to do on a Friday night
jokes.explanation: A functional self-own — Leslie's characteristic transparency betrays her loneliness. Not a big laugh but an honest, character-consistent moment that lands as a mild chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, Ben is... he's a great guy. Really great. And he's, you know, very capable. Competent. He has two hands and two feet, which is the standard amount. And he's never once tried to murder me, which I think speaks volumes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So yeah, we're just... we're colleagues. Professional colleagues who sometimes eat lunch in the same room. Coincidentally. Because the cafeteria only has so many tables.

jokes.text: Shauna's two headline pitches: 'It's the End of the World as They Know It, but Pawnee Feels Fine' (too long) / 'Zorp Shmorp. Doomsday Prediction Falls Flat as Citizens Spend Pleasant Evening Enjoying One of Pawnee's Finest Parks.' (somehow longer)
jokes.setup: Shauna pitches a headline for her story, Leslie notes the first one is 'a little long'
jokes.punchline: Her second attempt — framed as a correction — is demonstrably, absurdly longer while appearing to try to be shorter
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is clean: first headline is too long, second is worse. 'Somehow longer' as the observation is the right callback button. 'Zorp Shmorp' as the opening of a serious headline is also its own joke — Shauna deploying dismissive Yiddish-inflected slang in a newspaper headline. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why are you even talking to her? And don't say 'because she asked me a question' because that's a terrible reason.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What if you guys become friends? What if you become best friends? What if you decide to start a business together?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A bed and breakfast in the Poconos. What if it's very successful? What if you're on the cover of Innkeeper Monthly?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What if you fall in love? What if you get married on the cover of that same magazine?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And I'm not invited because I'm too busy being angry at you for ruining my life!

jokes.text: Shauna asks if Chris is single. Leslie says no, he's dating Jerry's daughter. Shauna says she meant Ben. Leslie's increasingly panicked non-answers about Ben.
jokes.setup: Shauna casually asks if a colleague is single, and Leslie assumes she means Chris
jokes.punchline: She meant Ben — Leslie's ex — and Leslie's spiral of non-answers ('He's a man, and he's a worker, and he is... We've never discussed sex') is a cringe comedy escalation revealing her emotional investment
jokes.explanation: Leslie's verbal disintegration under romantic stress is a reliable comedic engine for this show. 'He's a man, and he's a worker, and he is...' trails into nothing. 'We've never discussed sex' is the funniest evasion — framed as businesslike but revealing she's thought about it. 'Your guess is as good, nay, better than mine' is a great piece of flustered Leslie rhetoric.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, did you see that? The way he looked at her when she said 'the report is due Friday'? That's not just eye contact, Ben, that's a CONNECTION. She tucked her hair behind her ear. He blinked. Twice. That's basically a marriage proposal in body language. They're soulmates, I can feel it. We need to start planning the wedding. I'm thinking outdoor ceremony, string lights, maybe at that barn upstate...

jokes.text: 'He's a man, and he's a worker, and he is... We've never discussed sex, so... We've always just been very business-like, so your guess is as good, nay, better than mine.'
jokes.setup: Shauna asks if Ben is single
jokes.punchline: Leslie's attempt to sound neutral and professional completely collapses — 'nay, better than mine' is the key tell that she knows everything about him
jokes.explanation: The 'nay, better than mine' construction is the most precise bit of Leslie rhetoric in this sequence. By saying her own guess is WORSE than a stranger's, she ironically reveals intimate knowledge of Ben. The comedy comes from the gap between her performance of ignorance and her obvious emotional transparency. Strong Leslie characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my God, twenty bucks! This is it. This is my lottery ticket. I'm gonna be rich!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, actually, you know what? I found money on the ground. That was on my bucket list. Bucket list item: complete. I'm basically a lottery winner.

jokes.text: Leslie's spiral: 'I know how Shauna operates. She smiles, and then they fall in love, and then they get married, and then she changes her name to Shauna Malwae-Wyatt. Or he's going to be really progressive and change his name to Ben Wyatt Malwae-Tweep.'
jokes.setup: Leslie watches Shauna talk to Ben and immediately catastrophizes the romantic possibilities
jokes.punchline: She's already planned their marriage and argued the naming convention — including the progressive surname-swap scenario, which infuriates her on Ben's behalf
jokes.explanation: The escalation from watching them talk → marriage → name change → progressive surname swap is perfectly calibrated. The kicker — 'God, I am so annoyed that he would hypothetically do that' — reveals Leslie is already feeling possessive jealousy about a fictional event she invented 10 seconds ago. This is Leslie's anxiety and love expressed through absurdist projection. One of the episode's finest character jokes.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The sandwich is pretty awesome.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Awesome? April, this isn't just awesome. This is a bucket list item. I've been planning this moment for years. The bread has to be artisanal, the meat has to be heritage breed, and the condiments have to be applied with the precision of a Swiss watchmaker.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's a sandwich, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's not a sandwich, April. It's a SANDWICH. And I'm going to enjoy every single moment of this achievement.

jokes.text: 'God, I am so annoyed that he would hypothetically do that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just imagined Ben taking Shauna's last name in a hypothetical future marriage
jokes.punchline: She is genuinely, emotionally annoyed by an event she made up
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. The word 'hypothetically' is doing all the work — it's a perfect, precise acknowledgment that none of this is real, immediately undercut by the genuine emotional heat of 'I am so annoyed.' The compression (nine words of enormous comedic yield) is exceptional. Wholly Leslie, wholly specific, deeply quotable. Compares favorably to top-tier Parks character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hey guys, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, just about Shauna's new project.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's great, Shauna. You look really... fertile today.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: Um, what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean— your pants! Those are great pants. Very nice pants. I like the pants. The way they're on you. The pants.

jokes.text: Ann's deadpan: 'Oh, boy. Okay. Wow! I'm sure this is nothing.' — then immediately: 'Okay, well, that was definitely something.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says she needs to stop Ben and Shauna from getting together; we cut to Ann watching something happen between them
jokes.punchline: Ann's rapid reversal — 'I'm sure this is nothing' → beat → 'that was definitely something' — implies whatever she saw was unmistakable and happened almost instantly
jokes.explanation: The visual gap between Ann's two statements is the joke — something happened off-screen (or on-screen but not in transcript) that was unmistakably romantic. The structure of reassurance → immediate reversal is tight. 'Oh, boy. Okay. Wow!' as a three-beat reaction is well-performed comedy that implies escalating shock.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you can't leave! What about us? What about everything we've built together?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I have to go.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But think about how embarrassed you'll be!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My face would be melted off.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly! So embarrassing!

jokes.text: 'I know that move. They're going to have sex in five minutes.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been told 'that was definitely something' regarding Ben and Shauna
jokes.punchline: Leslie's assessment is specific ('I know that move'), clinical ('five minutes'), and reveals she has catalogued Ben's romantic signals
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'five minutes' is what makes this funny — not a vague prediction but a precise timeline derived from recognizing his move. It's both evidence of Leslie's emotional entanglement and a funny clinical detachment. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Their faces are all red.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: Actually, in a nuclear apocalypse, the faces would turn white from the flash burn, then blister and peel. The red comes later, after the initial radiation sickness sets in.

jokes.text: Andy and April's bucket list item: winning the lottery = finding a $10 bill on the ground
jokes.setup: Andy's bucket list includes 'win the lottery'
jokes.punchline: They interpret finding $10 on the ground as winning the lottery — 'Oh yeah! 10 bucks. That counts as winning the lottery.'
jokes.explanation: Andy's interpretation of his own bucket list goals with maximum generosity to himself is a running thread of this storyline. Finding a $10 bill 'counts as' winning the lottery because both involve receiving unexpected money. The logic is demented but internally consistent — very Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: Their faces just melted off. Like wax.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's not great.

jokes.text: The 'most amazing grilled cheese ever' bucket list item — 'My bucket list doesn't say make a pretty awesome grilled cheese sandwich.'
jokes.setup: April tries to convince Andy the grilled cheese they made is 'the most amazing grilled cheese ever made'
jokes.punchline: Andy's exacting standards for his own bucket list item reject 'pretty awesome' as insufficient — requiring the superlative from the list itself
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Andy's arbitrary standards — he's simultaneously easy to please (finding $10 = winning the lottery) and uncompromising about specific items. 'Pretty awesome' is not on the list; 'most amazing ever' is. The inconsistency reveals his childlike but sincere relationship with his own goals.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm not just a party planner, I'm a party scientist. I have a philosophy about parties. The key to a perfect party is that the party must start at the exact right time. If people arrive even five minutes early, the party hasn't started yet. But if they arrive five minutes late, the party is already over. It's all about precision.

jokes.text: Leslie trying to separate Shauna and Ben: 'Keep your pants on. What? I mean, keep your pants on, girl. I mean, those are really nice pants. Where did you get them?'
jokes.setup: Leslie runs over to interrupt Ben and Shauna's conversation and immediately says something that could be misinterpreted
jokes.punchline: Her attempt to recover from 'keep your pants on' digs deeper with each try — ending with an invitation to go pants shopping as a diversion tactic
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe-comedy verbal spiral: Leslie says something ambiguous, tries to clarify, makes it weirder, then pivots to complimenting pants as if that solves everything. The offer to 'go buy more pants' as an escape route is perfectly absurd. Leslie's social panic is endearing and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'd like to play a piece for you. It's called 'Requiem for a Thousand Exploding Suns, Opus 47 in B-Flat Minor.'

jokes.text: 'Because you can't go. I mean, what if you're not here when Zorp shows up? Boy, would your face be red. When Zorp shows up, your faces will be melted off and used as fuel.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is desperately trying to keep Shauna from leaving the cult vigil with Ben
jokes.punchline: She starts an idiom ('your face would be red') that Herb completes with the literal apocalyptic version — faces melted off and used as fuel
jokes.explanation: The collision between Leslie's idiom ('face would be red') and Herb's literal doomsday theology ('faces will be melted off and used as fuel') is a fantastic structure. Leslie sets up the conventional expression and Herb hijacks it with horrifying specificity. The phrase 'used as fuel' is genuinely disturbing and funny in equal measure. Good dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I read your books. They're very... imaginative.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, you're a real... what's the word... oh, you're bananicorn.

jokes.text: Herb's response to Shauna leaving: 'Wow, what an unbelievably unpleasant person.'
jokes.setup: Shauna politely declines Leslie's bizarre intervention and leaves for Tom's party
jokes.punchline: Herb — who preaches the apocalyptic burning of human flesh — judges Shauna as 'unbelievably unpleasant'
jokes.explanation: The irony is that Herb — a doomsday cult leader who believes in face-melting — is judging normal social behavior as unpleasant. The juxtaposition works well because he delivers it with total sincerity and conviction.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: When you die, you get reincarnated as another life form based on how you lived.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: You live a good life, you come back as something better. You live a bad life, you come back as something worse.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: Zorp lived a bad life. So he came back as a sinkhole.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head: 'The perfect party, it's an elusive idea... people have to be completely entertained from the moment they walk in until the moment they leave. It's a grand experiment, and I am a party scientist. Welcome to my laboratory.'
jokes.setup: Tom introduces the party concept with grandiose self-assessment
jokes.punchline: Calling himself a 'party scientist' and the club a 'laboratory' with a welcoming gesture — an absurdly inflated framing for what is a going-out-of-business bash
jokes.explanation: 'Party scientist' is a genuinely funny self-concept for Tom. The laboratory framing applied to a nightclub is appropriately delusional. Good character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, that sounds bad, but I think if we just get the Parks Department involved, we can probably find a solution that works for everyone.

jokes.text: The cult's flute performance is titled 'Symphony for the Righteous Destruction of Humanity in E Minor'
jokes.setup: A cult member plays a mournful flute piece at the vigil
jokes.punchline: Herb announces the piece name — 'Symphony for the Righteous Destruction of Humanity in E Minor' — which sounds like a genuine classical composition but is about the apocalypse
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'in E Minor' makes this. Doomsday cults don't typically compose in specific musical keys — the formal classical notation applied to apocalyptic subject matter is a perfect absurdist joke. 'Righteous Destruction of Humanity' as a composition title is also delightfully bureaucratic. High originality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, wait! I have an idea. What if we played a game together? A game so epic, so all-consuming, that you'll forget all about leaving Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, what kind of game?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Calvinball meets Catan meets fantasy football meets competitive bird watching. I call it... Caltanbird.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That sounds horrible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It gets better! Each turn takes six hours, and no one's ever actually won. The rules change every five minutes, and half of them are written in Esperanto.

jokes.text: Herb: 'Reminder. These flutes are available for purchase. You can't take it with you, people.'
jokes.setup: After an apocalyptic flute performance at the vigil
jokes.punchline: Herb uses the doomsday context ('you can't take it with you') to encourage flute purchases — the cult leader is helping Ron move inventory
jokes.explanation: This is a beautiful callback that rewards the earlier Ron/flute setup. 'You can't take it with you' repurposes the classic pre-death idiom in reverse — usually it means don't hoard wealth, here it means BUY NOW before you're melted by Zorp. The cult leader moonlighting as a salesman for Ron Swanson's woodshop is absurdist genius. Tight economy, strong callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, Ben, don't go! We could play a game!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I really need to get back to work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, wait — there's a gas leak! A gas leak in the building!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, no, scratch that — your car is being towed. Your car is being towed right now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, okay — the mayor is here. The mayor is here and he's asking for you specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, there's a swarm of bees! A biblical swarm of bees!

jokes.text: Leslie tells Herb his books are 'bonkersville' but pivots to sincere engagement about reincarnation
jokes.setup: Leslie has speed-read both of Herb's cult texts
jokes.punchline: 'Full disclosure, I think they're bonkersville' — Leslie's earnest civic vocabulary applied to apocalyptic cult literature
jokes.explanation: 'Bonkersville' is a perfect Leslie-ism — the kind of invented, slightly childish intensifier she uses. The combination of 'full disclosure' (professional language) with 'bonkersville' (made-up word) is quintessential Leslie voice.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We could do a fake hostage scenario.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to shoot you now.

jokes.text: Herb's reincarnation description pivots from beautiful to: 'you will take a new form. That of a fleshless, chattering skeleton when Zorp the Surveyor arrives and burns your flesh off with his volcano mouth.'
jokes.setup: Herb delivers what sounds like a genuinely touching meditation on reincarnation ('from the universe we emerge, and to the universe we return')
jokes.punchline: He pivots to the specific Zorp mechanics — fleshless chattering skeleton, volcano mouth — which ruins the spiritual beauty
jokes.explanation: Structural masterwork: the setup sounds genuinely moving — 'from the universe we emerge, and to the universe we return, infinite forms in infinite universes' — then pivots to 'chattering skeleton' and 'volcano mouth.' The juxtaposition between the cosmic beauty of the opening and the B-movie horror specificity of the ending is perfectly executed misdirection. 'Volcano mouth' is an exceptional piece of absurdist worldbuilding.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm doing this action movie scene, right? And I need a villain name. A Russian villain name. So I'm like... *Dimitri Volkoff*. No wait, *Sergei Petrov*. Actually, you know what? *Yuri Boombottom*.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'That was very strange, what you just said. I don't like it as much as that other thing you said.'
jokes.setup: Herb has just described everyone becoming fleshless chattering skeletons via volcano mouth
jokes.punchline: Leslie's measured, comparative critique — 'I don't like it as much as that other thing' — treats the apocalyptic vision as a speech quality issue rather than a theological horror
jokes.explanation: Leslie's gentle constructive-feedback framing of the apocalypse is a top-tier character joke. 'I don't like it as much as that other thing you said' is measured, diplomatic feedback on cult prophecy — exactly the kind of thing Leslie would say. Her instinct to manage the social moment even when faced with graphic doomsday imagery is perfect. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Help! I've been kidnapped by jewel thieves!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Now they're going to ravish me!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh God, and they smell like a bus station bathroom.

jokes.text: Leslie offers to play ChessRisk — 'half-chess, half-Risk, takes 15 hours to play' — to keep Ben away from Shauna
jokes.setup: Leslie sees Ben heading somewhere and desperately tries to distract him
jokes.punchline: Her diversion is ChessRisk — a game she invented that combines the two longest board games into something that takes 15 hours — which she presents as a 'fun game'
jokes.explanation: ChessRisk is a great invention — it combines the two most notoriously long board games, implying the 15-hour play time would keep Ben thoroughly occupied. The specificity (15 hours) is key. Leslie's desperation makes the absurdism land.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm like an action hero, but instead of bullets, I use... compliments. I'm gonna go give everybody a piece of my mind. And by piece of my mind, I mean a compliment. Boom. Nailed it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not how any of this works.

jokes.text: Leslie's frantic non-explanation: 'I forgot I have a thing I need to show you. It's so amazing. It's going to freak you out. It's something that we need to get in my car and go to.'
jokes.setup: Ben is about to leave to Tom's party and Leslie needs to stop him
jokes.punchline: Her cover story is 'a thing' — completely content-free, escalating in claims of amazingness while offering zero information, ending with the very suspicious 'in my car and go to'
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the vagueness escalating — 'a thing' → 'it's so amazing' → 'it's going to freak you out' → 'it's something we need to get in my car and go to.' Each sentence is more alarming and less informative. Ben reasonably going along with this speaks to his feelings for her.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, excuse me, I need to head out for dinner.

jokes.text: Tom brings out a surprise drumline at the party
jokes.setup: Tom declares the party needs to go to the next level
jokes.punchline: A full drumline marches in — absurdly elaborate for an intimate party that was empty minutes ago
jokes.explanation: A visual gag that works as escalation — Tom going from empty party to DRUMLINE is very Tom. Functional but not especially crafted in a transcript-readable way.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I've brought you to a very special place. This rock right here? The founding fathers definitely walked past this exact spot. Probably. On their way to somewhere important.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, this is just a parking lot behind a Arby's.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A HISTORIC parking lot behind a Arby's. Now come on, I want to show you where I think Ben Franklin might have tied his horse.

jokes.text: Tom calls for the drumline at the party: 'I think we've got to take things to the next level. Drumline, hit it.' [Drumline plays]
jokes.setup: Tom decides to escalate the party
jokes.punchline: Tom has hired a literal drumline for his party — an absurdly over-the-top and logistically impressive choice for a small club party
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the commitment — Tom actually got a drumline. Visual gag that lands on screen because of the sheer overkill. Rewatch bonus for the visual spectacle.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: According to my research, Mick Jagger was born in 1943, which would make him only 8 years old when he opened his first gas station in 1951.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, that's what the internet says!

jokes.text: April and Andy's action movie hostage scene — 'Just hold up this butter knife to my throat and pretend like you're holding me hostage'
jokes.setup: Andy is attempting to fulfill his bucket list item of being an action star
jokes.punchline: His method for becoming an action star is staging a fake hostage situation with a butter knife, in public, with a documentary crew
jokes.explanation: Andy's plan to 'become an action star' by acting out a scenario is great character logic — he believes performing the action will make him the thing. The butter knife specifically is a nice detail (not a real knife — the compromise between action and safety).

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You can't leave Pawnee. I won't let you. You're the only one who understands me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I love you. But I can't stay just because you need me to. That's not fair to either of us.

jokes.text: 'Just crazy enough to work.'
jokes.setup: April says the hostage plan 'seems a little crazy'
jokes.punchline: Andy delivers the action-movie cliché with total sincerity, using genre language to justify a completely silly plan
jokes.explanation: A well-worn cliché but Andy's earnest delivery in context makes it land. His goal to be an action star makes the genre phrase appropriate — he's becoming the character. Economy excellent; originality low.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Let's go to Mount Rushmore!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're going to Mount Rushmore aren't we? Even though we have no plan, no money, and it's a nine hour drive.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yep.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And we're leaving right now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Right now.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This is the worst decision we've ever made and we're both fully aware of it.

jokes.text: April as Janet Snakehole: 'He's stolen my jewels. And now he's going to ravish my body. And he stinks! He really stinks!'
jokes.setup: April is playing her alter-ego Janet Snakehole in Andy's action movie scenario
jokes.punchline: Janet Snakehole's distress escalates from stolen jewels to ravishment to 'he stinks!' — the final improvised complaint being completely un-cinematic and purely personal
jokes.explanation: The escalation from dramatic to mundane is perfectly structured: stolen jewels (classic) → ravishment (dramatic) → 'he stinks' (deflating and real). April's commitment to the bit and then breaking it with a genuine complaint is great character work. 'He really stinks' — the 'really' adding emphasis to this most personal grievance — is the best word in the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If I were reincarnated, I would want to come back as a socket wrench. It's useful, it's reliable, and it doesn't have to deal with people's emotions.

jokes.text: Andy's pun: 'Looks like this Siberian husky is going to be Russian off to jail.'
jokes.setup: Andy as Agent Macklin confronts the Russian villain in the action movie scenario
jokes.punchline: Andy delivers a pre-planned action-hero pun — 'Russian off to jail' (rushing/Russian) — which he had to be prompted to say
jokes.explanation: The pun itself ('Russian off to jail') is middling — not a great pun, but it's appropriately terrible for an Andy-scripted action movie. The setup that he needed to be told to 'say the line' implies he wrote this in advance and still almost forgot it. That meta-layer makes the weak pun funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not going to discuss my personal beliefs with you. That's between me and whoever I pray to, which is nobody. I don't pray. I don't believe in god. But if I did, I wouldn't tell you about it.

jokes.text: Jerry asks if he can go — 'Gayle is making a roast' — mid-action-scene
jokes.setup: The action movie scenario is still going; Andy has just delivered his pun
jokes.punchline: Jerry breaks character again to ask if he can leave for dinner, citing Gayle's roast — prioritizing his domestic life over both the roleplay and his coworkers
jokes.explanation: Jerry's running joke of having an inexplicably happy domestic life (Gayle, the roast) used to deflate a silly roleplay. 'Gayle is making a roast' as a reason to exit a fake hostage situation is perfect Jerry — his real life is better than the fantasy everyone else is performing. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Hey Lucy, it's Jean-Ralphio. Tom wanted me to call you.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.line: Oh my god, finally! Where has he been? We've been dating for three months!

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Dating? Oh right, right. Yeah, so Tom's been super busy with the business stuff. He asked me to tell you he's gonna be late.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.line: Late? Late for what? We had plans tonight!

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Oh, well he wanted me to let you know that... wait, you guys are dating? Since when?

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.line: Since May! Your best friend's been in a relationship with me for three months and you forgot?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Three months? Man, that's when I got really into snake charming. I've been so focused on that, I totally forgot.

jokes.text: Leslie's 'special place' is a gas station she believes Mick Jagger owned from 1951-1958 based on financial records showing 'M. Jagger' as owner — 'which, at first, I thought was a woman. Maybe Meg or something.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has dragged Ben to a 'special place' with great anticipation
jokes.punchline: The special place is a mundane gas station; her evidence that it's Mick Jagger's is 'M. Jagger' in financial records, which she initially thought was a woman named Meg
jokes.explanation: Leslie's research methodology — 'M. Jagger' = Mick Jagger, probably — is both absurd and perfectly consistent with her overenthusiastic approach to everything. The 'maybe Meg or something' detour shows she actually considered other options before settling on the Rolling Stones front man. The 1951-1958 dates are also perfect — Mick Jagger was born in 1943, making this theoretically possible and therefore impossible to fully disprove. Detailed absurdist character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: The end times are upon us. Civilization as we know it will crumble to dust. Famine, pestilence, and darkness will consume the earth.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: We have donuts in the break room.

jokes.text: Ron's response to what he'd want to be reincarnated as: 'Socket wrench sounds pretty good, actually.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just heard that Buddhists believe you could be reincarnated as a 'pretzel or a socket wrench' — and is asked what he'd choose
jokes.punchline: Ron, without hesitation, selects the socket wrench — finding more appeal in being a useful tool than a human or spiritual entity
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect Ron Swanson joke. The socket wrench is not exotic or spiritual — it's a practical, quality tool that does its job with no fuss. Ron's aspiration to be a socket wrench in the afterlife is a complete character statement compressed into six words. 'Actually' implies brief consideration, which makes it better. Exceptional character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I have to tell you something. I think I'm in love with Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's nice. Tomorrow's Friday though.

jokes.text: Ron on his religion: 'Well, I'm a practicing none of your...business.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks Ron what religion he is after he endorses the socket wrench reincarnation path
jokes.punchline: He starts 'none of your...' which sounds like 'none of your business' (rude dismissal) but is actually the religious category 'none' — those who practice no religion — with a pause to attach 'business'
jokes.explanation: This is the most structurally accomplished joke in the episode. 'A practicing none of your... business' operates on two levels simultaneously: (1) Ron identifies as a religious 'none' (no religion), which is technically accurate and sounds like a formal denomination, and (2) he converts it mid-phrase to 'none of your business,' his characteristic privacy reflex. The pause-and-pivot is perfect wordplay construction. Maximum information per word. Compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor example — this is tighter, funnier, and more character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm so miserable. Everything is terrible and nothing will ever get better.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: Well, the world is going to end in 2012. Might as well enjoy yourself now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you. That actually makes me feel so much better.

jokes.text: Ann's meditation on reincarnation: 'You spend so much time trying to figure out what you're going to be in the next lifetime that you forget to enjoy the one you're in now.' / Herb: 'Ann Perkins, that was beautiful.'
jokes.setup: Ann offers a genuine-sounding philosophical observation about the danger of reincarnation belief
jokes.punchline: Herb — the doomsday cult leader whose entire belief system is about the next existence — is deeply moved by this
jokes.explanation: The irony of Herb being deeply moved by advice that completely contradicts his entire belief system is quietly funny. 'Ann Perkins, that was beautiful' — the full name adds a touch of formal admiration that makes it sweeter and stranger. A soft joke but genuine.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, I'm gonna sleep for like the first 28 hours, okay? You're gonna do all the driving.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What? No. We agreed we'd both drive.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm really tired. Plus, I get car sick when I'm awake in a car.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You literally just slept for eight hours.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but that was sleep sleep. This is gonna be drive sleep. Totally different thing.

jokes.text: Tom's party talking head: 'Drumlines, personalized gift bags, tigers. This is the best party I've ever been to, and I'm not just saying that.'
jokes.setup: Tom is evaluating his own party mid-event
jokes.punchline: The list 'drumlines, personalized gift bags, tigers' — slipping 'tigers' in casually implies they actually have tigers at this party
jokes.explanation: The casual 'tigers' drop is the joke — buried between drumlines and gift bags, it's either true (they rented tigers) or an exaggeration Tom has convinced himself of. Either way, it's perfect Tom Haverford grandiosity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I may have orchestrated our entire relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I created situations where we'd run into each other, I may have sabotaged some of your dates, and I definitely planted that article about you in the Pawnee Journal.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But it worked! We're together now. We're making out. Next thing you know we'll be having babies and naming them after government buildings.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... a very specific escalation.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's confession: 'I actually forgot they ever dated. I was trying to hit that.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio has just done something thoughtful — calling Lucy for Tom — and Tom thanks him genuinely
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio reveals he had no idea Tom and Lucy had dated; his motivation was purely selfish romantic pursuit, not friendship
jokes.explanation: The reveal recontextualizes Jean-Ralphio's apparent act of friendship as accidental. 'I was trying to hit that' is delivered without guilt or embarrassment — which is more Jean-Ralphio than remorse would be. The subversion of the heartwarming moment into self-interest is a perfect character beat. Economy: the confession is two sentences, perfectly compressed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, Ben. I'm sorry, Shauna. I made up your entire interest in model trains. I invented it all. I literally created a false person.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And I'm actually really proud of how convincing I was.

jokes.text: Herb at the vigil: 'Last call for donuts.'
jokes.setup: Zorp's arrival is imminent — 20 minutes to the end of the world
jokes.punchline: The cult leader's pre-apocalypse announcement is about donut availability — treating the end of days as a catered event with refreshment logistics
jokes.explanation: Four words that are somehow hilarious. The cult managing donut logistics in the final minutes before Zorp melts everyone's faces is a perfect contrast. 'Last call' has dual meaning: a bar closing-time announcement, and also quite literally the last call before the end of human existence. The economy is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, where are the faces? I thought Mount Rushmore would be... bigger. And, you know, have faces on it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're on the wrong side of the mountain, dummy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that would explain why I don't see George Washington's beautiful face right now.

jokes.text: Leslie tries to confide in Ron: 'Can I speak with you about a personal matter?' / Ron: 'Normally, no. But given there's only 20 minutes until the end of human existence, also no.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ron if she can discuss something personal, framing the end-of-world context as a reason he might relent
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'normally, no... also no' structure suggests the apocalypse makes no difference to his stance on personal conversations
jokes.explanation: The structure here is exceptional: the expected punchline is that Ron would relent because it's the end of the world. Instead, the 'also no' maintains his position perfectly — the apocalypse changes nothing about his aversion to personal conversations. 'But given there's only 20 minutes until the end of human existence, also no' is a beautiful construction. Very high character integration — this is exclusively Ron's joke. Compares favorably to top-tier anchors.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Herb, you had one job. ONE JOB. And that job was to not mess up the calculations for the end of the world.

jokes.text: Ron: 'The sun's going to rise right over there. It will be a regular Friday, and you'll be in the exact same position you were in before.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is indulging apocalyptic feelings about her relationship with Ben
jokes.punchline: Ron cuts through all the emotion with a precise, boring prediction: it will be a regular Friday. His pragmatic certainty about the non-apocalypse is funnier than any emotional response.
jokes.explanation: Ron's gift for deflating emotional drama with mundane accuracy. 'A regular Friday' is the perfect Ron Swanson reframe — not comforting, not harsh, just factually boring. He's right, and that's what makes it sting and be funny simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: I need to reschedule the apocalypse.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, let me check the calendar. We have the end of the world penciled in for Tuesday at 2 PM. Would Wednesday work better for you?

dialogue.speaker: Herb
dialogue.line: Wednesday is fine, but I'll need the permits filed by Friday.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No problem. I'll get you the apocalypse application. It's the same form as the petting zoo, just with more fire.

jokes.text: 'If it makes you feel any better, Leslie, we'll all be dead in 20 minutes.' / 'That does make me feel better. Thank you, Herb.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says thinking about Ben with someone else makes her miserable
jokes.punchline: Herb offers the consolation that everyone will die in 20 minutes. Leslie genuinely accepts this as comfort. It works.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. The dark logic of 'everyone dies soon' as genuine emotional comfort is perfectly executed. Leslie's sincere 'That does make me feel better. Thank you, Herb.' accepting the doomsday consolation at face value is exactly right for her character — she needed this specific kind of perspective shift. The joke earns its darkness because it's also emotionally true for Leslie in this moment.

jokes.text: Andy and April have driven to Mount Rushmore — 'Where's all the faces? Like the presidents.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April drove to Mount Rushmore overnight from Pawnee — the implication is they're looking at the monument
jokes.punchline: Andy asks where 'all the faces' are — like the presidents — apparently from a vantage point where they can't see them, or in pitch darkness
jokes.explanation: The reveal that they drove to Mount Rushmore is already a great payoff for the bucket list storyline. Andy's failure to locate the famous carved presidents' faces — describing them as 'all the faces, like the presidents' — is both tourist-baffling and perfect Andy. He's at one of America's most famous monuments and can't find the thing.

jokes.text: Andy and April in the stolen car: 'The map says 30 hours, but I drive really fast.' / 'I didn't bring any music.' / 'I'll just take a real quick snooze for like 12 hours.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are in the car headed to Mount Rushmore
jokes.punchline: Three consecutive practical problems in a row: the trip is 30 hours (not a quick jaunt), there's no music, and Andy's solution is to sleep 12 of those hours — leaving April to drive alone for half the trip
jokes.explanation: Each of the three beats lands on its own: 30-hour trip (reality check), no music (oversight), sleeping 12 hours (Andy's selfish solution disguised as generosity — 'so I'm fresh'). The 'so I'm fresh' justification for abandoning April to solo driving is the funniest element. Good Andy character.

jokes.text: Leslie admits she took Ben to Mick Jagger's gas station because she was jealous of Shauna: 'Because she thinks you're cute, and I was afraid you guys were going to make out and have babies.'
jokes.setup: Ben confronts Leslie about why she really brought him to the gas station
jokes.punchline: Leslie's stated fear — 'make out and have babies' — leaps immediately to reproduction, bypassing any intermediate stages of a relationship
jokes.explanation: A decent callback to the jealousy arc — 'make out and have babies' as the compressed timeline of Leslie's fear is funny in its directness. Not as strong as the earlier jealousy jokes but serves the scene.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'And why don't you tell Shauna to make herself decent, and I'll apologize to her as well?' Ben: 'Oh, well, Shauna is not here.' Leslie: 'Oh. See what I did? I do. I'm very sneaky.'
jokes.setup: Leslie apologizes for her jealous scheming and tries to also apologize to Shauna
jokes.punchline: Shauna left — meaning Leslie's ploy worked — and Leslie can't resist a brief moment of pride before catching herself
jokes.explanation: 'I'm very sneaky' delivered with self-aware pride is a good Leslie button — she's simultaneously apologizing for her manipulation and unable to resist appreciating her own success. The pivot from contrition to smugness is fast and character-specific.

jokes.text: Andy at Mount Rushmore: 'Where's all the faces? Like the presidents.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April have apparently driven to Mount Rushmore — revealed as their spontaneous road trip destination
jokes.punchline: Andy is confused about where the faces are, seemingly not recognizing/seeing the monument directly in front of him — or unable to reconcile the real thing with his mental image
jokes.explanation: A beautiful Andy moment — 'Where's all the faces? Like the presidents.' implies he either can't find them (looking the wrong direction), doesn't recognize what he's seeing, or expected something more overwhelming. The 'Like the presidents' clarification (who else would Andy think Mount Rushmore had?) is perfectly redundant. High character integration — this line is pure Andy Dwyer. The visual gag of the camera presumably showing him standing right in front of the monument elevates it.

jokes.text: Herb returns to admit he made 'crucial errors' in his texts: the world ends May 19th. Leslie says the park is unavailable — Spring Spectacular ice cream giveaway. Herb immediately revises: 'I misspoke. Yeah, it's May 20.'
jokes.setup: Herb humbly admits his apocalyptic calculations were wrong and the real end date is May 19th
jokes.punchline: Leslie says the park is booked. Herb immediately and without hesitation revises the end of the world to May 20th — adjusting divine prophecy around the Pawnee parks schedule
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode-closing joke. The escalating absurdism of Herb adjusting the apocalypse around an ice cream giveaway is structurally flawless. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) it satirizes cult flexibility in prophecy, (2) it celebrates Leslie's bureaucratic competence overriding cosmic events, (3) it's a perfect Parks and Recreation joke — local government triumphing over the apocalypse through scheduling. 'I misspoke. Yeah, it's May 20.' delivered without missing a beat is exceptional. This is the episode's best structured joke and deserves a top score.

tmdb_overview: A local Pawnee group predicts the end of days, causing chaos in the Parks department.
insight: Doomsday panic spawns 65 jokes in 22 minutes—absurdist chaos over crafted setup.
